article.title: historical roots of white Christian nationalism
article.author: Dick and Sharon
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Christianity began with teachings about love, compassion, humility, and concern for the poor. Yet throughout history, rulers invoking the name of Christ have justified conquest, slavery, torture, and the destruction of entire communities. How did a religion rooted in the teachings of a man executed by an empire become one of history's most effective instruments of imperial power? That question animated a wide-ranging conversation between LA Progressive co-founders Sharon Kyle and Dick Price and Rev. Peter Laarman, a retired minister and longtime progressive Christian activist, about his recent article, “Christian Fingerprints on Europe's New World Crimes.” Laarman, who formerly led Progressive Christians Uniting in Los Angeles, is a member of the National Council of Elders and serves on its King and Breaking Silence team. The conversation began in 15th-century Spain but quickly expanded to encompass the origins of racial hierarchy, the enslavement of Africans, contemporary Christian nationalism, immigration enforcement, and the possibilities for transforming American political culture. When Christianity Became an Instrument of Empire Laarman explained that Christianity's entanglement with imperial power began long before Christopher Columbus sailed across the Atlantic. He traced a pivotal transformation to the fourth century, when Roman Emperor Constantine embraced Christianity and helped set the religion on a path toward becoming an instrument of state authority. Early Christians, Laarman observed, had represented something fundamentally different: a community that challenged domination and emphasized solidarity with the powerless. But as Christianity became associated with imperial authority, rulers discovered its usefulness in legitimizing their ambitions. That relationship reached particularly destructive heights under Spain's Ferdinand and Isabella. In their campaign to consolidate political power, the monarchs combined military conquest, religious persecution, and lavish public displays of Christian devotion. The Spanish Inquisition, led by figures such as Tomás de Torquemada, subjected suspected religious dissenters to torture and execution. Religious conformity became inseparable from political obedience. Laarman described the Inquisition's enforcers, including Dominican friars who proudly embraced the designation “Dogs of God,” as agents of an emerging authoritarian state. Sharon Kyle drew a comparison between Torquemada's relentless enforcement machinery and contemporary American immigration policies, particularly the role of Stephen Miller and ICE. The parallels, she suggested, were difficult to ignore: authorities identifying supposedly dangerous outsiders, normalizing harsh treatment, and invoking a higher political or moral purpose to justify their actions. For Laarman, the significance lies not in claiming that these historical episodes are identical, but in recognizing recurring patterns of domination. Related: Beyond Plantation Capitalism: Rev. Peter Laarman on the Fight for Economic Justice Columbus, Christianity, and the Origins of Racial Hierarchy One of the conversation's revelations concerned Christopher Columbus. Although Columbus is commonly portrayed as an ambitious navigator seeking a western route to Asia, Laarman emphasized his religious zeal. Columbus understood his voyage partly through the lens of Christian conquest. His ships carried crosses associated with the Crusades, and his ambitions were intertwined with dreams of expanding Christianity's reach. The same religious worldview that helped justify Spain's campaign against Muslims and Jews accompanied Europeans into the Americas. Laarman argued that the conquest of Indigenous peoples and the subsequent enslavement of Africans cannot be understood apart from the religious ideologies that legitimized European expansion. Sharon brought her own genealogical research into the discussion. Tracing ancestors through the Caribbean, she had encountered the Moravian Church and other missionary movements that brought Christianity to enslaved Africans. She wondered whether conversion had once offered enslaved people a potential route toward freedom. Laarman explained that Christian authorities and plantation owners found ways to separate spiritual equality from legal freedom. Enslaved people could be baptized without becoming free. He connected this contradiction to the development of racial categories that enabled Europeans to preserve systems of enslavement while maintaining Christian identities. The Spanish obsession with limpieza de sangre , or purity of blood, also helped establish precedents for later racial hierarchies. These developments, Laarman argued, demonstrate how religious distinctions could evolve into supposedly permanent distinctions based on ancestry. The discussion also explored how Portugal and Spain divided overseas territories, how plantation agriculture transformed the Caribbean, and how sugar became a powerful economic engine of the Atlantic slave trade. Christianity was not merely present during these developments. Religious institutions, interpretations, and authorities helped shape the systems through which conquest and exploitation operated. Related: Curbing Cancerous Capitalism: An Organizing Challenge for the Ages Is Violence Human Nature—or Something We Have Learned? The conversation eventually turned from historical atrocities to a more fundamental question. Are human beings naturally predisposed toward domination and violence? Sharon invoked the biblical story of Cain and Abel, asking whether humanity might be hardwired for conflict. Laarman resisted that conclusion. He suggested that even within the Bible, ethical understandings evolve—from images of a punitive, dominating God toward prophetic traditions emphasizing justice, solidarity, and compassion. Jesus, in Laarman's interpretation, continued that movement away from domination. Christianity's original ethical vision, he argued, was not about enforcing submission to earthly rulers. “We started with an anti-imperial, anti-domination proposition,” he said. He described an alternative tradition in which everyone belongs, everyone possesses dignity, and the poorest and weakest receive priority. Laarman also rejected the assumption that human societies must organize themselves through coercion and superior force. Although domination has become deeply normalized, he maintained that other ways of living and organizing society remain possible. The culture of violence, he suggested, is neither inevitable nor divinely ordained. Related: Marlon James Uncovers Depths of Depravity in Evangelical Christianity Beyond Trump: The Need for Transformational Politics Dick Price brought the conversation into the approaching American elections. Could the country reject not only Donald Trump but also the cruelty, resentment, and authoritarianism associated with his political movement? And would electing Democrats be enough? Laarman cautioned against confusing electoral victories with fundamental change. He distinguished between transactional politics—changing officeholders while preserving existing institutions—and transformational politics, which seeks to alter the underlying structures of power. Simply electing what Dick called another collection of politicians in blue suits would not necessarily address the country's deeper problems. Laarman recalled the excitement surrounding Barack Obama's promise of change, followed by disappointment when established financial and political interests retained substantial influence. Real transformation, he argued, requires more than campaign rhetoric. It requires changing governing institutions, challenging concentrated wealth, reforming congressional procedures, and organizing sustained public pressure. Sharon raised another concern drawn from her experience as a publisher: people often become politically engaged when a crisis directly threatens them, only to disengage once that immediate danger passes. She argued that offering a compelling vision of a better society is not enough. People also need to see what that society would actually look like and how it would work. Laarman enthusiastically agreed. The discussion returned to the New Deal, when organized labor and progressive movements helped push Franklin Roosevelt toward far-reaching reforms. Political leaders, the participants agreed, rarely produce transformational change without organized movements demanding it. Related: Recalling the Torments of a Radical Truthteller Reclaiming Christianity's Radical Promise Near the conversation's conclusion, Laarman was asked what single misconception about Christianity's role in creating the modern Western world he would most like to correct. His answer returned to Columbus and the European conquest of the Americas. Christianity was not simply the incidental religion of the explorers, he argued. A militant conception of Christianity as a conquering faith profoundly shaped their ambitions. That history matters because contemporary white Christian nationalism did not emerge from nowhere. It draws upon a centuries-old tradition in which religious identity becomes intertwined with national power, racial hierarchy, and the suppression of people deemed outsiders. But Laarman refused to concede that domination represents Christianity's essential character. The alternative remains available in the teachings of Jesus, the prophetic tradition, and the commitment to solidarity with society's most vulnerable. The conversation ultimately offered more than a critique of historical Christianity. It posed a challenge to the present. If religious institutions and political movements helped construct systems of domination, people can also organize to dismantle them. And if the culture of violence is learned rather than inevitable, another political and moral culture can be built in its place. Laarman described the possibility in terms that brought the conversation full circle: a politics of revolutionary love . Not merely a change of parties or presidents, but a transformation in how people understand their obligations to one another. That, perhaps, is the most important lesson to draw from Christianity's troubled history: the past need not determine the future, but understanding it is indispensable to changing what comes next. Watch the conversation with Rev. Peter Laarman, Dick Price, and Sharon Kyle, and read Laarman's original essay, “Christian Fingerprints on Europe's New World Crimes,” at LA Progressive.
